spreads.title: What August Looks Like
spreads.sub: Five dated obligations, and a widening gap between announced and verified.

spreads.title: Hassabis gave up the Gemini roadmap. Jeff Dean left the same week.
spreads.cap: Google DeepMind's London offices, where Hassabis stays on to advise without operational authority.
spreads.pull: Established: Hassabis no longer runs DeepMind day to day. Inferred: nearly everything else.

fact.label: years Jeff Dean spent at Google before leaving to co-found a research startup that Google itself is helping to fund.

body: August opened with an org chart. On August 5, Sundar Pichai and Demis Hassabis told Google DeepMind teams that Hassabis is stepping back from running the lab day to day, becoming Chair of Google DeepMind and Chief Scientist of Alphabet — a role the announcement framed around where artificial general intelligence is heading rather than the daily mechanics of shipping Gemini. **Koray Kavukcuoglu** becomes Senior Vice President, reports directly to Pichai, and takes over Gemini model development, frontier AI research, and the Gemini app and developer teams. Hassabis keeps Isomorphic Labs and stays available to advise from London.

Kavukcuoglu is not a steadying outside hire. He joined DeepMind in 2012 out of a PhD under Yann LeCun. ==The new title formalizes authority he was already exercising over Gemini's engineering; what changed is that Hassabis is no longer the person he answers to on it.== ++— continued overleaf ++

spreads.crosshead: The 30th employee walks, and Google writes one of the checks
spreads.cap: Four Google veterans, one public benefit corporation, and a thesis about running experiments in parallel.
body: The rest of his record is in-house: he co-developed the deep reinforcement learning behind AlphaGo, worked on AlphaFold and WaveNet, oversaw the 2023 merger of DeepMind and Google Brain, became CTO in 2024 and Google's Chief AI Architect in June 2025.

Jeff Dean — Google's 30th employee, its chief scientist, co-author of MapReduce, Bigtable, Spanner and TensorFlow — announced the same week that he is leaving after 27 years to co-found **Discovery Loop**, a public benefit corporation aimed at automating scientific and engineering research, starting with machine-learning research itself before expanding toward hardware design, drug discovery and clean energy. Sanjay Ghemawat, Oriol Vinyals and Quoc Le are going with him. Google is a founding investor and cloud partner, alongside Radical and Khosla. Dean's pitch for the approach: "You will get both a higher quantity and a higher quality of experiments, and that will lead to scientific breakthroughs and advances."

Alphabet shares fell nearly 4% on August 5, with the reshuffle and Dean's departure landing within hours of each other. The stock move is a measurable fact. The reason usually attached to it — concern about talent concentration and competitive standing against OpenAI and Anthropic — comes from market commentary, not from Google or Alphabet, neither of which has offered a public read. The two events are also formally separate: neither announcement mentions the other.

What August actually tests is narrower than the headlines. ==Kavukcuoglu now owns the Gemini roadmap alone, and how he uses it — faster iteration, a different research bet, or no visible change at all — is the only evidence that will show whether this reshuffle mattered beyond the org chart.== Discovery Loop, meanwhile, has shipped no product and disclosed no results. Four famous founders and a public benefit charter buy a thesis attention, not an outcome.

spreads.title: Microsoft is merging four Copilots into one login
spreads.cap: Four products, four launch dates, one sign-in — and one credential that now reaches source code and email alike.

fact.label: paid Microsoft 365 Copilot seats, on Microsoft's own disclosed count, against roughly 450 million commercial seats overall.

body: On Microsoft's fiscal fourth-quarter earnings call on July 29, Satya Nadella confirmed the consolidation in a sentence: "This quarter, we are bringing these Copilot experiences together, including code, in one 'super app' spanning both consumer and commercial experiences." What merges, by his own description: the consumer Copilot chat app, GitHub Copilot's code generation, Copilot Cowork, and **Autopilots**, a newer tier of long-running autonomous background agents wired into Agent 365, Microsoft's enterprise governance layer. He offered no interface details beyond that.

The fragmentation being undone wasn't a design error. It was chronology. ==Four products, four launch dates, four separate places a user's context and history lived — a GitHub session and an Office session shared no memory of each other, even for the same person on the same account.== ++— continued overleaf ++

spreads.crosshead: Growth off a small base, and a wider blast radius
spreads.cap: Agent 365, the governance layer Microsoft says will hold IT, security and finance sign-off in a single place.
spreads.pull: Fast growth off a small base and a large idle-seat problem can both be true at once.
body: The dates are the whole explanation. GitHub Copilot shipped in 2021, before ChatGPT existed. Microsoft 365 Copilot arrived bolted onto Office apps in 2023. Copilot Cowork — the multi-step workspace that reached general availability last month — is weeks old, and Autopilots is newer still.

Microsoft disclosed real growth on the same call: **over 30 million paid Microsoft 365 Copilot seats**, net seat adds more than doubling quarter over quarter, customers with more than 50,000 seats up more than sevenfold year over year, conversations per user nearly doubled, and time from deployment to heavy use down "from months to just days." Those are Microsoft's own figures, not a third party's estimate.

The backdrop is a gap. Fortune reported in May, citing an industry analysis, that fewer than 4.5% of Microsoft 365's roughly 450 million customers paid for Copilot at the time, with an estimated 20-30% of paid seats opened weekly — putting genuinely regular users nearer 1% of the base. Whether one app closes the distance between seats sold and seats used, or just makes seats easier to sell, is the question this merger exists to answer and hasn't yet.

Two cautions for August. OpenAI merged ChatGPT and Codex into one desktop app in July, and its president Greg Brockman said of the result: "It's kind of a mess. We agree." And Nadella's "this quarter" is Microsoft's fiscal Q1 2027, running through the end of September — ==trade coverage that rounded it to "by August" was press shorthand, not a date Microsoft stated.== The quieter change is identity: one credential now reaches source code, email, and whatever an Autopilot is authorized to touch unattended.

spreads.title: August 2, then August 31
spreads.body: Two transparency regimes became operative on August 2, one legislated in Sacramento and one in Brussels. Anthropic's Sonnet 5 introductory pricing ends August 31. The rest of this act is what happens in between.

spreads.title: Sonnet 5's introductory price ends August 31
spreads.cap: A rate change with a date on it, published on the same page as the thing that makes it bigger than it looks.
spreads.pull: A dated price increase is a rare object on this beat: no interpretation required, no benchmark to dispute, just a number that changes on a specific morning.

fact.label: per-token increase on both input and output when Sonnet 5's launch pricing ends, applied the same day with no phase-in.

body: Almost nothing in AI arrives with a date attached. Claude Sonnet 5's price increase does. Anthropic's own pricing documentation confirms the model reverts from **$2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens** to a standard **$3 and $15 on September 1** — a 50% rise on both rates, applied the same day, with no phase-in.

What doesn't revert is the token count. Claude 4.7 and later models, Sonnet 5 included, use a newer tokenizer that Anthropic's own documentation says produces roughly **30% more tokens for the same text** than the one Sonnet 4.6 and earlier used. ==From September 1 the two effects stack: a rate 50% higher, applied to a token count already about 30% higher.== Neither change is hidden — Anthropic states both on the same page. ++— continued overleaf ++

spreads.crosshead: Per-token prices keep falling. Per-task costs don't.
spreads.cap: The same request, the same job, more billable tokens underneath a price that looked unchanged.
body: The higher number is not new to Anthropic's lineup: $3 and $15 is identical to Claude Sonnet 4.6's standard rate, and the pricing page framed Sonnet 5's launch price as introductory rather than as a permanent discount. A developer who moved a workload from 4.6 to 5 to hold the per-token price flat was never paying an unchanged bill; more tokens were doing the same job under a sticker price that looked stable.

A disclosure, since this magazine runs on the thing it is describing: **the automated cycles that assemble this newsroom's daily coverage run on models in the Sonnet class.** The September rate applies to us the same way it applies to everyone else building on it, which is the reason we read the pricing page as closely as the launch post.

Read across the whole board and the direction isn't one-way. Anthropic held Opus 5 at $5 per million input tokens and $25 per million output on July 24, unchanged from Opus 4.8. DeepSeek's V4-Flash-0731 runs $0.14 and $0.28, with cached input — the unchanged part of a repeated prompt — discounted 98% to $0.0028. Alibaba is selling its Qwen3.8-Max preview at roughly 10% of expected standard pricing. Measured per token, intelligence keeps getting cheaper.

Measured per task, it doesn't. France's competition authority put a number on the other half of the equation in its July opinion: inference and orchestration costs have moved from roughly **4 cents per query in 2023 to about $1.20 per orchestrated task in 2026**. ==The unit got cheaper and the job got bigger, and agentic work bills by the job.== That is the arithmetic August hands to anyone budgeting for autumn — a falling price per token, a rising number of tokens per task, and one dated step change landing on the model class a great many agent workloads actually run on.

spreads.title: Four jurisdictions, one month, no coordination

fact.label: a day, the penalty that starts accruing the first day a covered provider is out of compliance with California's transparency law.

body: California's AI Transparency Act became operative on **August 2**. Any covered provider — a generative AI system publicly accessible in California with more than 1 million monthly visitors or users — now owes three things: a free public tool that tells anyone whether its own system made or altered content, an optional visible label, and a non-optional hidden machine-readable marker embedded in every image, video and audio file it generates.

The European Union's own Article 50 transparency duty took effect the same day. ==Legal trackers disagree on whether Sacramento timed its law to Brussels; the bill's own text never says.== ++— continued overleaf ++

spreads.crosshead: Brussels prises Android open; Beijing sorts agents into three tiers
spreads.cap: Voice invocation, cross-app actions, on-screen context, on-device models: the four layers Gemini has and its rivals don't.
body: The delay was California's own. The law arrived seven months later than lawmakers originally planned: it started as SB 942, signed in September 2024 with a January 1, 2026 start date, and AB 853, signed thirteen months later, pushed the date back and widened the net. The optional label is one a user attaches; the hidden marker has to carry provider, system, version and timestamp.

On July 16 the European Commission adopted a binding decision ordering Google to give competing assistants — ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity — the same system-level Android access Gemini currently holds exclusively. The Commission's stated rationale: roughly **60% of EU Android users** have no equal-footing alternative. The decision spans eleven Android features across four layers: invocation, actions, context, and resources, the last including Google's own on-device models. Search-data sharing is due January 2027; the Android interoperability changes by **August 1, 2027**. Non-compliance risks fines of up to 10% of Alphabet's annual worldwide revenue. Google had not issued a public statement on the July 16 decision as of publication.

China moved on a different axis. Implementation Opinions issued jointly by three national regulators — the Cyberspace Administration, the NDRC and the MIIT — sort every agent action into three tiers: decisions a user must make directly, decisions delegated to the agent by standing permission, and decisions the agent may take alone — with users retaining, in the framework's own words, "the right to know and the ultimate decision-making authority" across all three. Healthcare, transportation, media and public security face filing, compliance testing and product-recall provisions. ==The dating is messier than the deadline headlines suggest: trackers report compliance from July 15, one source traces issuance to May 8, and no penalty schedule or enforcement body has been named.== ++— continued overleaf ++

spreads.crosshead: 84%, 550 shopping queries, and a wall with almost no enforcement behind it
spreads.cap: The French regulator built its own agents and sent them shopping, logging what each one read against what it credited.
spreads.pull: The obligations arrived on schedule. Verification is still a volunteer activity.
body: France's Autorité de la concurrence published Opinion No. 26-A-05 on July 17: **OpenAI, Google and Anthropic together control more than 84% of the global AI agent market.** The authority didn't rest that on submissions. Between May 20 and 30 it built its own agents on the ChatGPT and Gemini APIs and posed 550 shopping-related queries, logging which sites each agent visited during research against which it actually cited. ChatGPT visited Reddit on 87.4% of discovery questions and cited it in 1.0% of final answers; Gemini cited the price-comparison site Idealo in 87.0% of purchase-completion answers. Traffic redirection from agent answers sits below 5% today; the authority projects it could reach 25% by 2030.

Beijing, meanwhile, is weighing whether its own models are an asset to protect rather than give away. The Financial Times reported on July 21 that the Ministry of Commerce is consulting Alibaba, ByteDance, Zhipu and chipmakers including Huawei about limiting foreign downloads of model weights and blocking transfers of training data abroad. Nothing has been decided, the FT's own reporting leaves the thresholds undefined, and Reuters said it could not independently verify the report.

==The wall is real and mostly unenforced.== The French opinion is advisory — it recommends enforcement, it doesn't impose it. China's agent framework names no penalty schedule and no empowered enforcement body. California's statute requires no provider to announce compliance at all, which means the only way to know whether a working detection tool existed on August 3 is for someone to upload a file and check, one upload at a time.

spreads.title: Every headline number on the board is the vendor's own
spreads.cap: Five benchmark wins, and no published list of which models were on the other side of them.

fact.label: new Claude models Anthropic shipped in under two months, leaving outside researchers less time than usual to test each one before the next arrived.

body: Anthropic released Claude Opus 5 on July 24 — its fourth new model in under two months, after Mythos 5, Fable 5 and Sonnet 5 — holding price flat at $5 and $25 per million tokens, unchanged from Opus 4.8. On Frontier-Bench v0.1 the model more than doubles Opus 4.8's score at a lower cost per task; on ARC-AGI 3 it scores **three times higher than the next-best model Anthropic tested**.

Every one of those numbers is Anthropic's own, and none has been independently replicated. ==The company doesn't publish which models it tested against on each benchmark, or under what prompting conditions — the detail that separates a real capability jump from a benchmark tuned to flatter the model that shipped it.== Treat the magnitude of the claim, not just its direction, as provisional. ++— continued overleaf ++

spreads.crosshead: An accusation with no evidence attached, and a score with no vendor behind it
spreads.cap: Roughly 1.4 terabytes of downloadable weights: Kimi K3, live on Hugging Face since July 27.
body: On July 22, Michael Kratsios, director of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy, posted that "We have information that Moonshot AI distilled Anthropic's Fable for the development of its K3 model." Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent followed within hours: "Open source is not open season on American IP." **Neither post included supporting documentation, and neither has been followed by a formal Commerce or Treasury filing.** China's embassy called the accusation "entirely unfounded"; Moonshot has not responded on the record. Independent researchers have publicly disputed that distillation alone explains a model of K3's scale and benchmark spread.

The claim isn't made from nothing. Anthropic disclosed in February that DeepSeek, Moonshot and MiniMax had run industrial-scale distillation campaigns against Claude through roughly 24,000 fraudulent accounts — more than 16 million exchanges combined. That disclosure named Moonshot's older Kimi line generally, five months before K3 existed. Drawing the line from that pattern to this specific model is what's new this summer, and it is the part no party has shown evidence for.

Separately, and settling a different question: Artificial Analysis, an evaluation outfit with no commercial stake in either party, scored K3 at **57** on its Intelligence Index — third overall, behind Claude Fable 5 at 60 and GPT-5.6 Sol at 59, narrowly ahead of Claude Opus 4.8 at 56. Anthropic's own claims sit on a different board: it says Claude Opus 5 beats Fable 5 outright on the OSWorld 2.0 computer-use benchmark at a third of the cost, a figure no third party has reproduced. The full weights went live on Hugging Face on July 27. ==The capability is independently verified. The provenance is not. Those are two claims, and only one of them has been measured.== ++— continued overleaf ++

spreads.crosshead: What to check in August, in order
spreads.cap: Fifty company names on a single policy letter, and the two conspicuous absences from the bottom of the list.
spreads.pull: Until Alibaba, or anyone else, publishes a table, second only to Fable 5 is a claim to note, not a result to cite.
body: The rest of the board runs the same way. Alibaba unveiled Qwen3.8-Max-Preview on July 19 — 2.4 trillion parameters, multimodal, positioned in the company's own material as "second only to" Claude Fable 5. ==No score table, no task-level results, no model card and no independent evaluation accompanied the announcement.== DeepSeek's V4-Flash-0731 claims to beat DeepSeek's own larger Pro model on agentic coding, and on DeepSeek's own suite it does: DeepSWE moved from 7.3 to 54.4. On the independent Intelligence Index, Pro still outscores Flash by six points. Both readings are true — they measure different capabilities — and DeepSeek's release post doesn't separate them for the reader.

The politics arrived in the same fortnight. Jensen Huang's first-ever post on X, on July 24, shared "Open Weights and American AI Leadership," a letter arguing Washington shouldn't restrict open-weight models; the roster roughly doubled to about 50 signers within a day, picking up OpenAI, Google, AMD and GitHub. **Anthropic and Amazon, its largest outside investor, are still not on it.**

Three checkpoints for the month, in order: whether any government publishes a forensic finding on K3, whether Treasury's threatened action ever actually lands, and whether an independent group replicates Opus 5's numbers before the next model arrives and resets the question.

spreads.title: Nine smaller stories worth knowing
spreads.intro: Not everything clears the bar for a feature. These cleared the bar for your attention.

items.t: Y Combinator open-sourced the agent harness it runs itself on
items.d: **QM**, MIT-licensed on GitHub, already handling YC's own accounting, legal, events and engineering work — including the work of building QM.

items.t: Google pulled a location-anchored image tool one day after launch
items.d: The Google Earth ==create image== feature anchored generated scenes to real satellite locations. Users faked a blast crater and staged protests at real mapped places; Google rolled it back inside a day.

items.t: OpenAI is opening its top model to 100,000 researchers
items.d: ChatGPT for Academic Researchers starts with 10,000 scientists this summer and $250 million behind it — the company's largest free-access commitment yet.

items.t: San Francisco gave Apple and Google 28 days to purge deepfake apps
items.d: City Attorney David Chiu's demand letters name 13 apps generating non-consensual nude images, citing California law on facilitating deepfake abuse.

items.t: DeepSeek quietly finished its cutover to V4
items.d: The old deepseek-chat and deepseek-reasoner aliases were permanently retired on July 24, forcing every integration onto the new line with no migration window.

items.t: Monzo's founder joined Anthropic to buy compute, not build product
items.d: Tom Blomfield took leave from Y Combinator for the compute team. The signal: securing capacity is now a founder-grade commercial problem, not a procurement line.

items.t: The White House is preparing a voluntary pledge on AI power costs
items.d: Reuters reports the administration wants commitments that data-center electricity costs will not be pushed onto existing utility customers. Voluntary, and not yet published.

items.t: A Kimi K3 zero-day claim went around with only half of it confirmed
items.d: Redis shipped seven security releases on July 23 fixing two real vulnerability classes. The claim that Moonshot's agents autonomously found 19 of them in ninety minutes traces to a single unverified source. ==The patches are confirmed; the discovery story is not.==

items.t: OpenAI launched an enterprise platform for deploying voice and chat agents
items.d: Presence bundles guardrails, permission controls and a review loop flagging where a deployed agent underperforms. Not self-serve — OpenAI's own engineers lead deployments.

spreads.title: Issue 001's calls, scored honestly
spreads.intro: Six went on the record last issue. One was graded then. Here are the other five, marked wins and losses alike — because a publication that grades itself all-correct is not grading anything.

items.t: GPT-5.6 reaches general availability by mid-to-late July.
items.d: Graded **RIGHT** in Issue 001 — Sol, Terra and Luna opened to all users on July 9, inside the window.

items.t: Terra's pricing forces a public reprice from Anthropic or Google inside a month.
items.d: **WRONG.** Opus 5 launched July 24 with pricing held flat at $5 and $25 per million tokens, unchanged from Opus 4.8. No reprice came from either company — and Anthropic's next dated pricing move is an ==increase==, not a cut.

items.t: US labs answer Chinese model share with price cuts, not benchmark campaigns.
items.d: **WRONG.** The highest-profile US response of the window was Opus 5: a benchmark campaign at unchanged pricing, which is precisely the move this call bet against. The price cutting that did happen came from Alibaba and DeepSeek — the other side of the board.

items.t: Meta's three-to-six-month agent payoff window slips at least once more.
items.d: ==Still pending.== The window runs to roughly October–January from Zuckerberg's early-July remarks. Nothing this month moved it either way.

items.t: Agility's or Unitree's filings show per-unit utilization far below the depreciation schedule.
items.d: ==Still pending.== Neither has published quarterly figures as a newly listed entity. The FCC's Covered List action complicates Unitree's US market access before any such filing arrives.

items.t: China's minors-protection provisions are the first component a Western regulator copies.
items.d: ==Still pending, and looking weaker.== The Western rules that did land — California's transparency act, the EU's Article 50 duty — are disclosure regimes, not minors-protection copies. China's own notable export this month was an agent-authorization framework nobody has copied yet.
